title: Torres urges CASA advocates to push through ongoing challenges in immigrant communities
summary: It's been a challenging year for immigrants, but they have faced adversity before and survived and will do so again, said Gustavo Torres, the outgoing executive director of the immigrant-advocacy group CASA at its 40th anniversary gala Thursday.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters November 7, 2025

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters November 7, 2025

The deaths of six immigrants who were working on the Francis Scott Key Bridge when it collapsed. The Trump administration’s “erroneous” deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia. Increased enforcement by federal immigration agents looking to boost deportation numbers.

Those are just a handful of challenges and turmoil that Maryland’s immigrant communities have faced over the last two years.

But at the 40th anniversary celebration Thursday for the immigrant-advocacy group CASA, outgoing Executive Director Gustavo Torres said that immigrants have overcome pain before and they will overcome current and future challenges – even if he is no longer at the helm.

“We didn’t start here. We didn’t start as a national powerhouse,” Torres, who could not attend the event in person, said over a livestream. “We didn’t start with policy wins or national campaigns. We started with pain; we started with injustice. We started with a handful of people who said ‘enough.’”

The 40th anniversary celebration was held at CASA’s Baltimore Welcome Center, which was filled with well over 100 advocates and lawmakers.

The celebration was also largely centered around Torres’ 34 years of work with the immigration advocacy group, helping both lawfully present and undocumented immigrants get connected to resources, while pushing for better conditions in the community.

Torres started working with the organization with three people in a church basement in Montgomery County in 1991, sixyears after its founding.

Today, he said CASA has 250 staff members, with its headquarters in Prince George’s County’s Langley Park neighborhood, home to one of the D.C. area’s highest concentrations of Latinos. More than three decades after he started, Torres will be passing the torch and retiring this month.

He said he has faith that members of the immigrant community will support each other on the road ahead.

“None of this happened by accident. It happened because we organized. It happened because we refused to give up. It happened because we believe in each other,” Torres said.

“Some years pass in the blink of an eye. One day, you are holding a baby at a rally. The next day, that baby is leading the rally,” he said. “I have learned from the elders who came before me, and now I look around and realize I am one of them.

“I see the next generation, and know we are in such good hands. We have won so much, but we have also hurt. We have been scared. We have been doubted and that’s OK,” Torres said. “Because fear is not new. Pain is not new. But neither is our power. The answer to fear is strength.”

During the celebration, Gov. Wes Moore (D) praised Torres for his time with CASA.

“Gustavo is someone with a loving heart, but a fighting spirit,” Moore said at the event. “Gustavo is someone who saw potential of a small team running out of a basement in Takoma Park Presbyterian Church … Those issues from 40 years ago, they haven’t gone away.”

Later, Del. Deni Taveras (D-Prince George’s) presented Torres with a citation from Moore, who left the event early. The citation was presented for Torres’ “demonstration of high integrity and ability, meriting our great trust and respect.”

“You’ve always been able to move the needle forward, and for that I thank you,” Taveras said during a toast for Torres.

When Torres came on-screen to deliver his remarks, he reminded the crowd that “it has never been about me, it has always been about you” and issued his own toast.

“To us,” he said. “Forty years of struggle, hope and solidarity. To the friends we have lost and the ones we have yet to meet. To the young who will carry this fight when we are tired. CASA has always belonged to the people.”

He then led the crowd in a chant of “Si, se puede,” a common rallying cry in immigrant settings that translates to, “Yes, you can.”
